questions.scenario: A team standardized its Claude Code coding conventions in a CLAUDE.md file that each developer keeps in their own home directory (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md). A new engineer joins, clones the repository, and starts Claude Code in the project, but is not following any of the team's conventions.
questions.stem: What is the MOST effective fix with minimal ongoing maintenance?

options.text: Ask the new engineer to copy the conventions file into their own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md by hand before starting work.
Install the conventions as a managed policy CLAUDE.md on the new engineer's machine so they cannot be excluded locally.
Move the conventions into ./CLAUDE.md (or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md) at the repository root and commit it, so it loads for anyone who works in the repo.
Have the team lead paste the conventions into the conversation at the start of each session in the repo.

questions.explanation: User-level memory (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`) is personal and never travels with the repository. Project-level `CLAUDE.md` is committed to git and loads at launch for every developer working in the repo, so the conventions arrive automatically with the clone and stay in sync.

whyWrong.A: Works once, but it is manual, easy to skip, and drifts out of sync with the team's copy.
whyWrong.B: Managed policy CLAUDE.md is an org-wide control deployed via endpoint management; it is the wrong scope for one team's conventions.
whyWrong.D: Conversation-only instructions are lost between sessions and must be repeated every time.

questions.mindset: Match the scope: team-shared behavior lives in files committed to the repo.

questions.scenario: A developer runs /init in a large legacy repository. Claude Code analyzes the codebase and generates a CLAUDE.md that runs to several hundred lines, including build commands, architecture notes, coding conventions, and verbose file-by-file commentary.
questions.stem: What should the developer do next to get the most value from the file?

options.text: Commit it unchanged, since /init output is curated by Claude Code and should not be edited by hand.
Review and trim it to the highest-value, stable instructions (targeting under roughly 200 lines), removing verbose commentary and details that change often.
Split it into a CLAUDE.md in every subdirectory so that each directory's guidance loads at launch with the session.
Delete it and re-create the content as a skill, so the conventions are loaded on demand instead of every session.

questions.explanation: `/init` produces a starting point to review and edit, not a finished artifact. Everything in CLAUDE.md costs context in every session, so the documented guidance is to keep files concise (a target of under 200 lines per file), keeping only stable, high-signal instructions and pruning verbose or frequently changing detail.

whyWrong.A: /init output is a draft to review and edit, not a protected artifact.
whyWrong.C: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load lazily when Claude reads files there, not at launch — and splitting alone does not reduce the volume of guidance.
whyWrong.D: Standing, universal project standards are exactly what CLAUDE.md is for; skills are for task-specific, on-demand workflows.

questions.mindset: /init writes a starting point — curated context beats dumped context.

questions.scenario: A monorepo's root CLAUDE.md stays concise by using @imports to pull detailed standards from docs/: API guidelines, database conventions, review checklists, and test standards. Developers notice that every session still pays the full token cost of all that imported content, even for tasks that touch only one area of the codebase.
questions.stem: Which change BEST reduces standing context usage while keeping each set of guidance available where it applies?

options.text: Restructure the imported documents so they nest more granularly under each other, reducing the size of each individual import.
Move all imported content into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which is loaded more efficiently than project-level imports.
Keep the imports but wrap each imported section in XML-style tags so Claude reads only the sections relevant to the current task.

Replace always-imported area standards with path-scoped files in .claude/rules/ (using paths: globs) that load only when matching files are read, and move task-specific workflows into skills that load on demand.

questions.explanation: @imports organize content but do not save tokens: they load at launch like the rest of the file. The on-demand mechanisms are path-scoped rules (which load when Claude reads a matching file) and skills (whose full body loads only when invoked). Routing guidance into those mechanisms is what actually cuts standing context cost.

whyWrong.A: However you rearrange imports, they still load at launch; nesting granularity does not change the token cost.
whyWrong.B: User-level memory is loaded the same way and costs the same context — it just makes the content personal instead of shared.
whyWrong.C: Tags improve readability and separation, but tagged content is still in the window; they do not make anything load on demand.

questions.mindset: Imports organize; only on-demand mechanisms (path-scoped rules, skills) save tokens.

questions.scenario: A platform team must guarantee that a pinned default model and a set of permission deny rules apply to every Claude Code session in the company, and that no engineer can remove or weaken them from project, personal, or command-line configuration.

options.text: In managed-settings.json deployed through endpoint management, which no user, project, or command-line setting can override.
In .claude/settings.json committed at each repository's root, since project settings outrank every other scope.
In ~/.claude/settings.json distributed by a bootstrap script, since user settings apply to all of a developer's projects.
In the root CLAUDE.md of each repository, instructing Claude to always use the pinned model and never perform the denied actions.

questions.explanation: Settings precedence is managed > command line > local > project > user. Only managed settings cannot be overridden from any lower scope, so organization-wide enforcement belongs there. Deny rules placed there also hold in every permission mode.

whyWrong.B: Project settings are outranked by local (`.claude/settings.local.json`), CLI, and managed settings, so engineers could override the pin.
whyWrong.C: User settings are the lowest file scope; any project or local file wins.
whyWrong.D: CLAUDE.md is injected context that guides the model; it is not enforced by Claude Code, cannot pin models, and cannot grant or revoke permissions — and it would have to be copied into every repo anyway.

questions.mindset: Enforcement that must survive user preferences belongs in managed settings.

questions.scenario: A project's committed .claude/settings.json contains permissions.ask: ["Bash(git push *)"]. To stop being prompted for routine pushes, a developer adds permissions.allow: ["Bash(git push origin main)"] to .claude/settings.local.json. Pushes to origin main still prompt every time.
questions.stem: Why does the prompt still appear, and what is the correct fix?

options.text: Allow lists from lower-scoped files are ignored; the developer must add the allow rule to the committed project settings instead.

Rules evaluate deny → ask → allow and the first match wins regardless of specificity, so the broader ask rule fires first; the fix is to remove or narrow the ask rule, not to add a more specific allow.
Allow rules in settings.local.json only take effect after Claude Code restarts, so the developer just needs to relaunch the session.
The allow entry is invalid because Bash permission rules cannot include arguments — only bare tool names are allowed.

questions.explanation: Permission rules are evaluated in the order deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins — a more specific allow never beats a broader ask, even one written in a lower-scoped file. Because the ask rule `Bash(git push *)` matches the command, the allow rule is never consulted. The fix is to adjust the ask rule itself (or accept the prompt).

whyWrong.A: List-valued keys like permissions.allow merge across scopes; the local allow rule is genuinely in effect — it just loses on evaluation order.
whyWrong.C: Local settings apply without a restart; restarting changes nothing about rule precedence.
whyWrong.D: Bash rules support command patterns with wildcards, such as `Bash(git push *)`; bare names are not the only valid form.

questions.mindset: Deny → ask → allow, first match wins — specificity never reorders evaluation.

questions.scenario: A team's CLAUDE.md includes "Never modify files under secrets/ and never run destructive shell commands like rm -rf." After an incident in which Claude deleted a directory during a cleanup task, the lead wants a guarantee that this cannot recur.
questions.stem: What is the MOST reliable control?

options.text: Move the rule to the top of the root CLAUDE.md and format it prominently so it is always read before anything else.
Add an instruction that Claude must restate the safety rules and confirm before running any destructive command.
Keep every session in plan mode permanently, so no edits or commands execute without explicit approval of a plan first.
Add permission deny rules — Edit path rules covering secrets/ and Bash deny patterns for destructive commands — which Claude Code enforces deterministically in every permission mode.

questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement: it guides the model but has a non-zero failure rate. Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code itself, and deny rules apply in every mode, including bypassPermissions. For guarantees, use enforcement mechanisms, not instructions.

whyWrong.A: Position and formatting do not make an instruction deterministic; it is still advisory context.
whyWrong.B: Asking the model to self-check is probabilistic and adds no enforced gate.
whyWrong.C: Plan mode is a working style for exploration and large changes, not a permanent safety control — approved plans still execute, and routine tasks become unusable.

questions.mindset: Context is advisory; permissions are enforced by Claude Code, not the model.

questions.scenario: A team created .claude/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md, which generates release notes from merged pull requests. Its description is "Helps with releases." Claude never picks the skill on its own when asked to draft notes for the new version; team members always have to invoke /release-notes manually.
questions.stem: What is the best FIRST fix?

options.text: Rewrite the description and when_to_use to state concretely what the skill does and when to use it ("drafts release notes from merged pull requests"), since the description is what Claude sees when choosing a skill.
Add several examples of good release-note output inside the SKILL.md body so the model recognizes the pattern and selects it.
Set disable-model-invocation: false in the frontmatter, because skills default to manual-only invocation.
Move the skill to ~/.claude/skills/, where personal skills take priority and load more eagerly.

questions.explanation: Progressive disclosure means only skill names and descriptions sit in context each turn; the body is invisible until the skill is invoked. A vague description like "Helps with releases" gives Claude nothing to match against the request, so improving the description is the direct fix.

whyWrong.B: Examples in the body help output quality after invocation, but the body is not in context when Claude decides whether to use the skill.
whyWrong.C: Skills are model-invocable by default; `disable-model-invocation` is not what is blocking selection here.
whyWrong.D: Personal skills only win priority on name conflicts — priority does not affect automatic selection, and it would un-share the skill from the team.

questions.mindset: The description is the interface Claude uses to select skills.

questions.scenario: A support engineer uses a custom /diagnose-logs command that walks Claude through reading and searching several large log files. The exploration floods the main conversation with thousands of lines, crowding out the actual work. She wants to keep invoking it as a command while keeping the main context clean.
questions.stem: Which change BEST meets that need?

options.text: Add allowed-tools: [Read, Grep] to the skill's frontmatter so it uses only cheap, read-only tools.
Set disable-model-invocation: true on the skill so its noisy output is no longer produced automatically.
Set context: fork in the skill's frontmatter so it runs in an isolated subagent and returns only a summary to the main conversation.
Run /clear immediately after each /diagnose-logs invocation to reset the conversation to an empty state.

questions.explanation: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated subagent context: the verbose exploration stays out of the main conversation and only the result comes back. This is the designed mechanism for keeping noisy, exploratory output from polluting the main window.

whyWrong.A: `allowed-tools` pre-approves tools for the turn — it does not actually restrict the skill to those tools, and either way it does nothing about the volume of log content reaching the main conversation.
whyWrong.B: The skill is already user-invoked; disabling model invocation changes nothing about the context it produces when run.
whyWrong.D: /clear wipes the whole conversation — including the actual work — rather than isolating the exploration.

questions.mindset: context: fork keeps exploration out of the main window.

questions.scenario: In a long session, a developer asks a code-reviewer subagent (.claude/agents/reviewer.md) to "check the auth changes." The subagent re-reads files from scratch, misses decisions made earlier in the conversation, and duplicates analysis the main session already completed.
questions.stem: What is the root cause and best fix?

options.text: The subagent inherited the full conversation but skipped over it; strengthen its system prompt to instruct it to follow prior context.
Subagents start with a fresh context and never see the parent conversation; pass what they need — file paths, decisions already made, what to skip — in the delegation message itself.
The subagent is missing memory: project in its frontmatter; enabling it lets the subagent read the main session's conversation memory.
Increase the subagent's maxTurns so it has enough budget to rediscover everything the main session already found.

questions.explanation: A (non-fork) subagent runs in its own context: no parent history, no earlier tool results, and only its final message returns to the parent. The delegation prompt is the only channel for context, so anything it needs — paths, decisions, scope boundaries — must be written into the task message.

whyWrong.A: Subagents do not inherit the conversation at all; there is no prior context for a prompt to reference.
whyWrong.C: The memory frontmatter controls which memory directories load (user/project/local memory files), not the parent conversation's history.
whyWrong.D: More turns just makes the duplicate work more thorough; it does not transfer the missing context.

questions.mindset: Subagents start fresh; the delegation prompt is the only channel.

questions.scenario: Yesterday a developer ended a productive refactoring session, named refactor-payments, in a project directory. Today she opens a terminal in the same project and wants to pick that exact conversation back up. Several other sessions have run in the project since yesterday.
questions.stem: Which approach reliably reopens that specific session?

options.text: Run claude --continue, which reopens the most recent session in the project directory.
Run claude --continue --fork-session so a fresh copy of the named session's history continues in a new session.
Start a new session and ask Claude to read yesterday's transcript file and reconstruct the context from it.
Run claude --resume refactor-payments to reopen the named session directly, or select it from the resume picker.

questions.explanation: `--continue` always reopens the most recent session in the directory and takes no name; `--resume <id|name>` targets a specific session (or opens a picker when given no argument). Since other sessions have run since, only resume by name or ID reliably reaches refactor-payments.

whyWrong.A: --continue ignores names and reopens the latest session, which is now a different one.
whyWrong.B: --continue still selects the latest session; the fork flag copies whatever that is, not the named session.
whyWrong.C: Reconstructing from a transcript is lossy and unnecessary when sessions are resumable by name or ID.

questions.scenario: A CI job runs Claude Code to label pull requests. The job hangs whenever Claude requests permission for a tool, and the log output is free-form text the pipeline cannot parse. The team needs the run to finish unattended and emit a machine-readable result.
questions.stem: Which change best meets BOTH requirements?

options.text: Run the job with claude -p and --output-format json, pre-approving only the tools it needs via --allowedTools (or setting --permission-mode dontAsk) so no prompt can stall the run.
Set CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true in the job environment so Claude Code skips all permission prompts and emits JSON output.
Launch the interactive CLI in the runner, accept every tool once with "don't ask again," then post-process the transcript into JSON with a converter script.
Use claude --batch to run the prompt without prompts and write structured logs to the job's artifacts directory.

questions.explanation: `claude -p` runs a single prompt non-interactively, `--output-format json` returns machine-parseable result and session_id, and `--allowedTools` (permission-rule syntax) pre-approves a minimal tool set — with `--permission-mode dontAsk` guaranteeing that anything not pre-approved is denied rather than hanging the run.

whyWrong.B: CLAUDE_HEADLESS is not a real setting; an environment variable cannot conjure headless behavior or JSON output.
whyWrong.C: Interactive acceptance in a CI runner is fragile, does not scale to fresh runners, and still yields unstructured output.
whyWrong.D: --batch does not exist; the non-interactive mode is `-p` / `--print`.

questions.mindset: Headless runs need non-interactive approvals and machine-readable output.

questions.scenario: A team is deciding which Claude Code files to commit so that anyone who clones the repository immediately gets shared behavior: a reusable command and the company's internal MCP server.
questions.stem: Which TWO locations, when committed to the repository, are shared with the whole team? Choose TWO.

options.text: .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md, which creates the /deploy command for anyone working in the repo.
.claude/settings.local.json in the repo root, holding personal allow rules for each developer.
.mcp.json at the repository root, defining the project-scoped MCP server configuration.
~/.claude/commands/deploy.md, the personal variant of the deploy command.
CLAUDE.local.md at the repo root, kept out of version control with a gitignore entry.

questions.explanation: Files under the repo's `.claude/` (plus CLAUDE.md and `.mcp.json`) are committed and shared with the team: project skills/commands run for everyone in the repo, and `.mcp.json` is the project scope for MCP servers. Everything under `~/.claude/` is personal, and `*.local` files are deliberately per-person.

whyWrong.B: settings.local.json is the personal, gitignored scope — the "local" in its name is the point.
whyWrong.D: ~/.claude is the user's home directory; those commands exist only on one machine.
whyWrong.E: CLAUDE.local.md is the personal, this-project-only layer meant to be gitignored.

questions.mindset: Committed repo files are shared; ~/.claude and *.local are personal.

questions.scenario: A developer relies on /rewind to undo mistakes and wants to understand exactly what checkpoints can and cannot restore before trusting them as a safety net.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about Claude Code checkpoints are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Checkpoints capture file changes made through Bash commands such as rm and mv, so shell mistakes can be undone with /rewind.
Checkpoints do not capture file changes made through Bash commands or by external programs; those must be undone with git.
Checkpoints are a full replacement for git in repositories where Claude Code does most of the editing.
Checkpoints persist with the session, so restores remain available after resuming that session later.
Checkpoints track edits made by most subagents, including work done in their isolated contexts.

questions.explanation: Checkpoints are a conversation-level safety net: they persist with the session (so they survive resume) and can restore code and conversation. They explicitly do not track file changes made via Bash, external edits, or most subagent edits, and they are not a replacement for git.

whyWrong.A: Bash-driven file changes (rm, mv, cp) are not captured by checkpoints.
whyWrong.C: The documentation is explicit that checkpoints are not a substitute for version control.
whyWrong.E: Most subagent edits are not tracked by checkpoints; revert those with git.

questions.mindset: Checkpoints are conversation-level safety nets, not git.

questions.scenario: A security reviewer is hardening a GitHub Actions workflow that runs Claude Code against pull requests. The goals are least privilege for tools and safe credential handling.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices should the workflow apply? Choose TWO.

options.text: Run with --permission-mode bypassPermissions inside the runner so no permission request can stall the job.
Commit a .claude/settings.local.json containing the job's allow rules so every fork uses identical permissions.
Pre-approve only the tools the job needs using --allowedTools with permission-rule syntax, such as "Bash(git diff *)" and Read.
Store the API key as a plaintext repository variable so fork pull requests can authenticate without secrets access.
Keep the credential in the CI secret store (e.g., GitHub Secrets) and inject it into the job's environment at run time.

questions.explanation: Unattended runs should pre-approve a minimal tool set via `--allowedTools` (permission-rule syntax), and credentials belong in the CI secret store, injected at run time — never committed or exposed in plaintext.

whyWrong.A: bypassPermissions is for isolated containers or VMs only and abandons least privilege entirely.
whyWrong.B: settings.local.json is the personal, gitignored scope; committing it is an anti-pattern and is not how shared permissions are distributed.
whyWrong.D: A plaintext repo variable exposes the key to anyone with read access; secrets stores exist for exactly this reason.

questions.mindset: Least privilege plus secrets in the secret store.

questions.scenario: A developer switches an interactive session to auto mode to reduce prompt fatigue and wants to know which guarantees still hold before trusting it on a sensitive repository.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about auto mode are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask and deny rules from permission settings still apply; auto mode does not bypass them.
Auto mode behaves identically to bypassPermissions, approving every action without any review.
Auto mode must be enabled by an administrator in managed settings before it can be selected at all.
A background classifier reviews each action in place of per-action prompts, and actions it judges unsafe still come back to the user for approval.
Auto mode only reviews file edits; shell commands always prompt exactly as they do in default mode.

questions.explanation: Auto mode replaces repeated prompts with classifier review, but it is a permission mode, not an approval bypass: deny and ask rules are evaluated before the permission mode and still apply, and actions the classifier deems unsafe are still surfaced to the user rather than executed silently.

whyWrong.B: bypassPermissions skips prompts wholesale; auto mode substitutes classifier review and still respects ask/deny rules.
whyWrong.C: Auto mode is a built-in selectable mode (the default start mode in recent versions); administrators can disable it via managed settings, but no enablement is required.
whyWrong.E: The classifier reviews actions generally, including shell commands — it is not limited to edits.

questions.mindset: Auto mode reviews instead of prompting, but ask and deny still rule.
